newsitem.title: Italy: TENNIS-KOURNIKOVA MAKES WINNING START AS SELES SOUNDS OFF.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-KOURNIKOVA MAKES WINNING START AS SELES SOUNDS OFF.

text.p: Fifteen-year-old Russian Anna Kournikova made a winning start at the Italian Open women's tennis tournament on Monday as attention focussed on what passes for a generation gap in the sport.

The first day of the 54th championships started with one Rome newspaper describing the women's event as a battle between "Lolitas and old stars" and the former teen-sensation Monica Seles discussing pushy parents and prodigies.

Kournikova, the youngest player in the draw who turns 16 in June, beat Taiwan's Wang Shi-Ting 6-4 6-3 after just over an hour on centre court before a sparse crowd and occasionally threatening-looking clouds overhead.
She then left the clay court to field questions with all the aplomb of an old pro swatting aside training balls.
"I felt pretty comfortable out there," the pigtailed Russian said confidently, wincing as she slowly eased an enormous sticking plaster delicately off her right shin.
"Its a pulled muscle, nothing really serious," she explained cheerfully to general disbelief.
"I have a lot of fun, Its been wonderful. I don't have any pressure on me at all," added Kournikova.
While the Russian clearly belonged to the ranks of the precocious, former world number one Seles enjoyed a bye and found herself cast as the mature veteran at 23.

The American, who won in Rome as a 16-year-old Yugoslavian newcomer in 1990 when she beat Martina Navratilova, returned to the Foro Italico for the first time in five years and gave a news conference as the voice of experience.
"I've learned not to expect much from kids," she said when asked how she felt about the new generation of youngsters led by Switzerland's 16-year-old world number one Martina Hingis.

"What I don't like at all is parents putting their children as soon as they are born on a tennis court and forcing them to like tennis," said Seles, who at 17 had been the youngest world number one in history before Hingis emerged.
"Sixteen-year-old kids just want to have fun and I think that's what they should do," she said.
Hingis, who would have been the big crowd-puller here after losing in last year's final to Spain's Conchita Martinez, is absent after falling off her horse last month.

Seles has not played in Rome since 1992, the year before she was stabbed on court in Hamburg by a spectator during an interval between games. She was 17 and the incident left mental scars that took years to heal.
This year Seles is the top seed and she said she had overcome recent injury and had been training for two weeks.
She faces Austria's Barbara Schett in her opening match late on Tuesday under floodlights and is set to meet France's 10th seed Mary Pierce in the last 16.
"I got a very tough draw," Seles insisted. "There are very good players even in the first rounds."
All the four seeds in action on Monday won through.
France's 15th seed Nathalie Tauziat beat Helena Sukova 6-4 6-2 while Belgian 13th seed Sabine Appelmans beat Naoki Sawamatzu of Japan 6-3 6-1.
Ninth-seeded Brenda Schultz-McCarthy of the Netherlands beat Henrieta Nagyova of the Czech Republic while 12th seed Elena Likhovtseva of Russia beat France's Anne Sidot.
